data.title: Turčianska Blatnica – Plešovica, a cult hillfort in Turiec
data.excerpt: A hillfort on the narrow, exceptionally sharp ridge of Plešovica above Blatnica in Turiec, at spot height 683, where the extreme number of hoards points to a cult site rather than an ordinary settlement. The objects deposited here span the Bronze Age to the Roman period, and the bronze Celtic helmet of the Berru type probably comes from the surroundings of Blatnica too.

children.text: Above the village of Blatnica in Turiec, running from south-west to north-east, stretches a mountain ridge about 1.5 km long called Plešovica. To the east it adjoins the Gaderská dolina valley, to the south and west Blatnica, and to the north it is separated by a narrow and deep saddle from the main mountain ridge, on the last spur of which stand the ruins of Blatnica Castle.

The hillfort lies at the lower end of Plešovica, at spot height 683. It is an elongated, very sharp ridge, almost level along its longest axis, but so narrow that there is scarcely room on it for an uncomfortable path. On every side it falls away unusually steeply, to the east and to the south even in a vertical rock face. Access is possible only from the saddle on the side of Blatnica Castle. At its southern end the ridge widens a little into a small, sloping platform. Geologically Plešovica belongs to the formation of the Choč dolomites and limestones. The natural security of the hillfort is very nearly perfect. On the eastern, southern and western sides a vertical rock face bars access into the hillfort. On the north-western and northern sides there is in turn a slope of great steepness. Only from the north-east can it be entered, along the ridge.

The rampart defences are adapted so as to prevent access precisely along the ridge. The rampart, 63 m long, is therefore at its most massive and highest in the part where access is easiest. There it reaches a height of up to 4 m on the outer side and 1 m on the inner side. The other ramparts have similar features; they allow for the possibility that an enemy who had approached along the ridge might succeed in bypassing the first line of defence. By their position the ramparts thus follow the character of the terrain, which can best be seen from the contour plan. They are built of material obtained on the spot. The hillfort has an area of about 1,700 m². Despite the fact that the area of the hillfort and the configuration of its interior are not entirely ideal for habitation, the hillfort must have held an exceptional position in antiquity, evidently one of a cult character.

children.text: Among the first to investigate the hillfort was Štefan Janšák, who is also the author of the first sketch of the defences. In modern times the hillfort has been studied chiefly by the archaeologists L. Veliačik and K. Pieta, but no more detailed excavation has yet been carried out here. In the area of the hillfort, as well as throughout the area of the summit ridge of the hill and its terraced slopes to the west, north-west and north of the hill, a large number of hoards of the Late and Final Bronze Age have been found. According to unverified information, hoards of the Hallstatt period were also found here. The traces of occupation identified during survey also testify to an exceptionally long-lasting occupation of this important site. Throughout the area of the hill, including the defences on its summit, pottery and metal objects were identified besides the prehistoric finds, ranging from the Bronze Age to the beginning of the Migration Period. Objects were also found on Plešovica that point to occupation of this site at the end of the Hallstatt period and at the beginning of the La Tène period. Both older and more recent finds include bronzes of the Orava group of the Hallstatt period. A two-part bronze brooch with a cup-shaped foot and a long spring is a rare find in the territory of present-day Slovakia. In the western Hallstatt milieu these brooches are a typical representative of the final phase of the Hallstatt period. Finds of the later La Tène period, recovered from the interior area of the hillfort, are strongly represented and consist of brooches of plain composite construction with the bow bent above the spring and with an external chord.

The supra-regional importance of Blatnica and of the hillfort on Plešovica itself is underlined by the numerous hoards deposited within the enclosure of the defences, but also over an extensive area on the slopes of the hill, which justifiably evoke a cult dimension to this place. At the upland sites of Stredná and Rovná no occupation of this period is attested. Červený grúň, less than four kilometres from Blatnica, was probably a satellite hamlet with certain features of a refuge, but also with traces of craft production. The hillfort of Blatnica-Plešovica and the hamlets around it remained an important place of occupation in the Iron Age as well, when, as at Folkušová, an agglomeration of sites formed here. It consisted of the hillfort and open settlements at its foot, which were linked (by an old route of unknown date) with the refuge on the hill of Rovná. At various places here hoards as well as stray finds from the end of the Hallstatt period and from the early and the older La Tène period were found.

children.text: The extreme number of hoards of the Late and Final Bronze Age, but also of the Hallstatt period and the older La Tène period, as well as the deposits of Celtic weapons in the wider area of Blatnica, draw attention to the special position of this place within the surrounding landscape over many centuries. Hoards and stray artefacts of the Late to Final Bronze Age (weapons, jewellery) occurred along a stretch almost a kilometre long, on the slopes and on the summit of the hill of Plešovica. An extensive assemblage of bronzes acquired in the 1870s also comes from Blatnica. Besides objects of the Bronze Age it also includes local ornaments of the Hallstatt period, as well as objects and hoards of the early to older La Tène period. A bronze Celtic helmet of the Berru type of the same date, which likewise entered the collections of the national museum in Budapest in 1879, probably comes from the surroundings of Blatnica.

children.text: The find of a La Tène sword in its scabbard with a suspension chain in the mountain terrain at Blatnica-Tisová, as well as the new, as yet unevaluated finds of weapons and ornaments from the foot of Plešovica in the locality known as Rémová, of the Late La Tène and the Early Roman period and including human bones, broaden our insights into the as yet undefined cult practices in the area of Blatnica. The weapon deposits from Blatnica were not professionally documented, but their location can clearly be regarded as credible. Without objective find circumstances we can therefore consider the interpretation of these remarkable finds only hypothetically. In the case of the weapons from Blatnica we are probably dealing with cult practices such as trophaea – dedications of captured weapons or votive offerings of another purpose. It is possible that these rituals continued an old tradition, perhaps a thousand years long, of a sacred place in the surroundings of the hill of Plešovica. Deformed shield bosses, brooches and other objects of the second half of the 2nd century AD from Rémová may be evidence of the continuation of this long tradition, which perhaps ended with the break in the continuity of occupation of the mountain region caused by the removal or departure of the Púchov population at that time. The enduring importance of the site is also attested by the well-known early medieval princely grave discovered at Blatnica-Sebeslavce in the 19th century.

children.text: The phenomenon of the worship of deities in a mountain environment, through the deposition of both intact and ritually deformed objects at places described as natural sanctuaries, but also at upland sites that cannot be explained at present, is common to many mountain ranges and to several periods. It is attested from earlier prehistory almost to the present day. These practices in the form of deposits – votive offerings – and their placing in the landscape have been the subject of study especially in the Alpine countries.
